newsitem.title: USA: USDA to compensate more U.S. wheat growers.
newsitem.headline: USDA to compensate more U.S. wheat growers.

text.p: The U.S. Department of Agriculture will offer a compensation package to wheat growers in the southeast United States where Karnal bunt spores have been discovered, the special assistant to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Wednesday.

But Paul Drazek, special assistant to Glickman, told the annual meeting of the Wheat Quality Council here that he was not at liberty to discuss the contents of the compensation rule prior to its publication.
"We're going to be as generous and flexible as we possibly can," Drazek said in a teleconference call from his Washington D.C. office.
Karnal bunt is a fungus which does not pose a health risk to consumers, but can affect the taste of wheat and wheat-based products. Its effect on wheat yields is not fully known.

Karnal bunt spores were discovered in Alabama, Georgia, Florida and Tennessee last year as a result of a USDA national survey that was prompted by the discovery of Karnal bunt in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and California.
Drazek said USDA had been "very close to issuing regulation on the handling of the situation in the Southeast and decided not to do it."
The USDA uses the term "regulation" to describe the quarantine measures it has taken in the southwest United States, where Karnal bunt was found last March.
Drazek said that department officials changed their minds about issuing regulation on handling grain in the southeast after meeting with members of the Alabama Congressional Delegation.
"As a result of that meeting and subsequent discussions with members of Congress from Georgia and Tennessee, we did some rethinking about the whole thing," Drazek said.

Drazek told the Wheat Quality Council that he knew there would be "some criticism" of the USDA for not regulating the Southeast. But he said USDA would likely have drawn more flack had it gone forward with the regulation.

Feed grain sources from regulated areas of the Southwest United States told Reuters on Wednesday that the Alabama Congressional delegation put extreme pressure on USDA not to issue regulation in the southeastern United States, unless a generous compensation package could be offered.
